chapters.title: Homophones
chapters.snippet: Their, there and they're sound the same but mean different things - tricky twins of the English language!

questions.definition: Words that sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings.
questions.example: There, their and they're are homophones.

questions.definition: 'Their' = belonging to them. 'There' = in that place. 'They're' = they are.
questions.example: They're putting their coats over there.

questions.definition: 'To' = towards. 'Too' = also or very. 'Two' = the number 2.
questions.example: I want to go too, but it is too late for two of us.

questions.definition: 'Were' = past tense of be. 'Where' = which place. 'Wear' = to put on clothes.
questions.example: Where were you when I wanted to wear my coat?

questions.title: Rocks Come in Three Kinds
questions.body:
Are all rocks the same? Not at all! Rocks can be smooth or rough, tiny or huge, grey or red. Scientists sort rocks into three kinds by looking at how they were made: sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic.

Sedimentary rocks are made from sand, mud, shells and tiny pieces of other rocks that settle at the bottom of rivers, lakes and seas. Over many thousands of years the layers are pressed together until they harden. These rocks often feel grainy and can crumble easily. Sometimes they even hold the print of a plant or an animal - a fossil.

Igneous rocks begin as hot, melted rock called magma. When magma cools and hardens, it becomes igneous rock. Granite and basalt are igneous rocks, and so is obsidian, which looks like black glass.

Metamorphic rocks are rocks that have been changed. When heat and pressure deep in the Earth squeeze an older rock, it turns into something new and very hard. A rock can change from one kind to another again and again. Scientists call this the rock cycle.

questions.title: Hiding and Standing Out
questions.body:
Plants and animals have a hard job: they have to stay alive in a wild world. Over a very long time, many of them have changed in clever ways to survive.

Some animals use camouflage. Their fur or skin is almost the same colour as the place they live, so hungry hunters, called predators, find it hard to see them. A deer's brown coat blends in with the trees. A rabbit in a snowy place may grow white fur in winter and brown fur in summer.

Other animals mimic something else. A walking stick insect looks just like a twig, so birds fly right past it. Some moths have spots on their wings that look like the eyes of an owl, which can scare a predator away.

Not every living thing wants to hide. Many plants grow bright flowers to stand out, because the colours attract bees that carry pollen. Some plants grow sharp thorns, and a porcupine has spines on its back. These protect them from anything that tries to eat them.

“Ibu, why do we eat rice every day?” Bayu asked, poking at his plate.

“Because we grow it here,” said Ibu. “The weather is warm and wet, which rice loves. There is plenty to go around.”

“Do children everywhere eat rice?” “No. Some places are too cold or too dry to grow it. So rice is put on ships and trucks and sent to them. And their apples and wheat are sent to us.”

Bayu stared at the shiny red apple in the bowl. “This apple travelled here?” “Yes, all the way across the sea,” Ibu smiled. “Food and many other things are made or grown where it is easiest, then sent to where people need them.”

“Wow,” said Bayu. “I never knew my lunch had such a long journey!” He took a big bite of his apple. “It tastes even better now.”

She took a deep breath and pushed the bookshelf aside. Behind it was a small hole, and inside the hole sat a family of tiny owls, huddled together and humming in their sleep!

questions.title: Two Seasons in Indonesia
questions.body:
Many countries have four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. Indonesia is different. Because it sits close to the equator, it is warm all year round, and it has just two seasons: the dry season and the rainy season.

The dry season lasts from about May to October. There is less rain, the sky is often blue, and the winds blow from the south-east. Farmers harvest crops such as rice, and children fly kites in the open fields.

The rainy season arrives around November and stays until April. Dark clouds gather in the afternoon, and heavy rain can fall for hours. Rivers grow full, and the rice fields turn bright green. In some places, floods can happen, so people clear their drains early.

Although the temperature changes only a little, the two seasons shape how people live. They decide when to plant, when to harvest and even when to celebrate.

Long ago, a poor fisherman named Pak Joko lived by the sea. Every morning he rowed out in his small boat and cast his net. Some days he caught many fish; other days only a few.

One morning, while he was mending his net, his knife slipped from his hand and sank into the deep water. Pak Joko was upset. The knife was old, but it was the only one he had.

Suddenly, a kind sea spirit rose from the waves holding a shiny golden knife. “Is this yours?” she asked. Pak Joko shook his head. “No, mine is plain and rusty.” Next she showed him a silver one. “That is not mine either,” he said.

At last she held up his old knife. “Yes, that is mine! Thank you!” Pleased with his honesty, the spirit gave him all three knives. Pak Joko shared the silver and golden ones with his village and lived happily for the rest of his days.

questions.title: How Bees Make Honey
questions.body:
Honey is one of the sweetest foods in the world, and it is made by bees. It takes a lot of teamwork.

First, worker bees fly from flower to flower and drink a sugary liquid called nectar. They store it in a special 'honey stomach'. A single bee may visit hundreds of flowers in one day.

Next, the bees return to the hive and pass the nectar to other bees. These bees chew it and mix it with a special juice from their bodies. The mixture is placed in small wax cells.

Finally, the bees flap their wings to blow warm air over the cells. This dries out the water, turning the thin nectar into thick honey. When a cell is full, the bees seal it with a lid of wax to keep the honey fresh.

questions.title: Komodo Dragons
questions.body:
The Komodo dragon is the largest lizard in the world. It lives only on a few islands in Indonesia, including Komodo and Rinca. A full-grown dragon can be three metres long and weigh as much as a grown man.

Despite its heavy body, the Komodo dragon can run fast over short distances and is also a good swimmer. Its long yellow tongue flicks in and out to taste the air, helping it find food from far away.

Komodo dragons are carnivores. They eat deer, wild pigs and sometimes even buffalo. A dragon's bite carries germs, and its prey usually becomes weak and cannot escape.

Today, there are fewer than 4,000 Komodo dragons left in the wild. The government has made their islands a national park to keep them safe. Visitors can watch them, but must stay with a ranger.
